t.1.63.1: O Rambhā, this very great task for the gods must be done by you: the seduction of Kauśika here, filled with desire and infatuation.
t.1.63.2: O Rāma, thus addressed by the wise thousand-eyed one, that apsaras, abashed, joined her palms in reverence and replied to the lord of the gods.
t.1.63.3: O lord of the gods, this great sage Viśvāmitra is terrible; he will unleash his terrible wrath upon me, O god, of that there is no doubt. That is why I am afraid, O god; please be gracious to me.
t.1.63.4: To her, trembling and with palms joined in reverence, the thousand-eyed Indra said: "Do not be afraid, Rambhā; may good fortune be yours. Carry out my command."
t.1.63.5: In the month of Mādhava, when the trees are lovely, I will become a heart-captivating cuckoo and, together with Kandarpa, will stay by your side.
t.1.63.6: O Rambhā, assume a form endowed with many charms and supremely radiant, and break the resolve of that ascetic sage Kauśika.
t.1.63.7: Having heard his words, she, graceful and sweetly smiling, assumed a form of unsurpassed beauty and set about tempting Viśvāmitra.
t.1.63.8: He heard the sweet sound of a cuckoo calling, and then, with a mind thrilled with delight, he gazed upon her.
t.1.63.10: Having understood that deed of the thousand-eyed one, the foremost of sages, the son of Kuśika, filled with anger, cursed Rambhā.
t.1.63.9: Then, at its call and its incomparable song, and at the sight of Rambhā, the sage was filled with suspicion.
t.1.63.11: Since you tempt me, Rambhā, who seek to conquer desire and anger, you shall stand as a stone for ten thousand years, O ill-fated one.
t.1.63.12: A brāhmaṇa of exceeding great splendour, endowed with the power of austerity, will deliver you, O Rambhā, defiled as you are by my wrath.
t.1.63.13: Having spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra of great splendour, unable to restrain his anger, fell into deep anguish.
t.1.63.14: By his mighty curse Rambhā then became a rock; and Kandarpa, having heard the words of the great sage, departed.
t.1.63.15: Once his austerity had been stolen away, O Rāma, that greatly radiant one, his senses still unconquered, found no peace within himself because of his anger.
